en: You mean to bury me myself.
The wild asses of the rolling hills—
I find I cannot chase them.
Though I thought I had a child,
I find I am a barren old head.
Drink stones, not spirits, Manas!
My thousands upon thousands, my great wealth,
You scatter across the open waste.
If that is not enough, your father's blood—
Mix it in and drink, Manas!
You made broth for your companions, Manas;
You slew my countless beasts by thousands, Manas!
Where are the swarming myriad herds?
Where is productive Altay?
We used to live side by side—
Where are the black Kalmyk people, Manas!
You caught and slaughtered my mares;
You repaid me for some far-off wrong.
You have terribly drained my strength.
The countless herds I kept in Altay,
You staked my livestock as prizes;
You have drained my strength!
When my herds would match my peers',
You chased and slaughtered my mares,
And repaid me for some far-off wrong!
Taking my livestock by force,
You have greatly drained my strength!
You catch and slaughter for the poor
Whose dirt one cannot touch by hand,
My good, gentle livestock.
The childless have peace of mind.
This oppression by Manas—
I seem to have come to witness it.
Parted from my many herds,
I seem to have come to die.
You have ended all my laughter;
You spent and squandered
My countless stores and possessions!”
When Khan Manas heard this,
He sprang up like a white tiger.
At ill-intentioned Jakyp,
He took offense, losing all hope.
Without speaking, without a word,
His stubborn anger gripped him fully,
His white teeth, broad as a door,
Teeth unlike other people's,
He ground again and again.
“With my father Jakyp, jealous of his herds,
Why should I squabble?
Let me put his livestock in his hands
And go elsewhere!
With Jakyp, jealous of his wealth,
Why should I make a scene?
If I have eaten up his wealth and herds,
Let me go elsewhere!
With my ill-intentioned father,
Why should I bicker?
However much of his property I have spent,
Let me wander among other peoples!
The four corners of the circle—
If I do not scout them four times over,
The five corners of Medina—
If I do not go round them five times,
May I die without being Manas.
Rather than bristle and quarrel,
Rather than stand contending,
Let me sink away as if unborn.
Rather than merely live in this world,
Let me expend all my strength,
And through the eighteen thousand worlds
Let me travel and tread!
Zhelpinish, Zhet-Kayt, the ends of the earth—
Wandering round them seven times,
Seeking a back to lean upon,
Seeking a renowned and mighty lion,
One who could be my equal,
Seeking a warrior mountain-like in presence,
One complete on every side—
Since my own strength is insufficient,
Let me seek and find
A twin, a companion equal to myself.”
Without anyone knowing,
Without anyone seeing,
He dipped his hands in water
And performed their ablution;
He dipped his feet in water,
And performed their ablution.
“Grant me a road where I am headed!”
Praying to the Creator,
The leopard grew fierce.
“You made all twelve of my members whole.
O Almighty, what can I do?
You made me a lion to slaughter unbelievers.
‘You squandered my livestock,’ he says—
You made me so unworthy in my father's eyes!
My father Jakyp, jealous of his herds,
That hero never sated with livestock—
Let me comply with what he says.
Whom ears have heard and eyes have seen,
Of all the warriors who fight,
Let me drive their livestock here
And give it all to my father!
Let me open his door wide;
Let me fill Jakyp's
Hole that stretches far away!
‘He scattered a little of my livestock,’ he says,
And acts unlike a human being,
Using force beyond a beast's.
My ill-intentioned father's
Wishes in this, let me grant.
Countless treasures, many gold coins—
If livestock is what he longs for,
Let me gather it for my father.
My ill-intentioned father's
Grievances, heard three times a day—
How can I sit and watch?
Let me gather peerless steeds in rows.
Those born of the same nest as my father—
Of eight of them there is no news.
Where ears have heard and eyes have seen,
Let me search the face of the earth!
One that will not tire in six months' riding,
Let me find among beasts and mount.
An untiring swift steed,
And one to share death and life with me—
Let me find a worthy kinsman!”
Thus speaking, Khan Manas
Grew fierce and gathered his force,
Against ill-intentioned Jakyp,
Deeply offended, he spoke:
“My protector, Kozhosan,
You used to say, ‘I will help, I will help’;
Now take me beneath the arm!
My dervish named Khizir,
You said you would be my companion;
Take my lead-rope and scout my road.
Father Shay, head of the forty chiltens,
My own father has become my enemy;
You yourself accompany me!”
Your lamenting blue-maned hero,
At Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
While the people lay in deep sleep,
Fierce and girding himself,
That surpassing lion born fortunate,
Mounted and rode out from Talas.
At the head of Besh-Tash lies Bek-Zhayloo;
He crossed over Bek-Zhayloo.
Beyond it lies Anzhiyan;
He traveled through Anzhiyan.
The pale plain of Anzhiyan—
When he reached that pale plain,
Straight before him he met
A white-bearded dervish.
The dervish stood and said:
“You are my champion, my warrior,
Born above other mortals,
My champion, my blue-maned lion!
Turn your horse's head and wait;
Stand in the place ahead awhile!
‘He has moved here from Altay,’ they said;
I knew that you would come,
Youngest of the six lions,
The servant beloved of Allah.
I, an old man, beyond measure,
Have wandered grieving in the waste!
You are my sultan, my support;
By the decree the Creator inscribed,
You are my lion who will shake the world.
Your first forefather was Khan Tügöl;
From your roots you were blessed by Khizir.
Where you spent a night and passed,
A lasting shrine was established.
Your first forefather, the saints
Accompanied and protected.
Your remote ancestor was Khan Tümön;
From Khan Tümön came Khan Sanchy,
From Khan Sanchy came Khan Böyön,
From Khan Böyön came Khan Chayan,
From Khan Chayan came Khan Ogoy.
How could Ogoy be an ordinary man?
Where that fair-skinned one had not trodden,
No whole tract of land remained;
Where Ogoy had not thrust and conquered,
No whole people remained.
He traveled along the River Lop.
Before your champion forefather Ogoy,
The enemy who faced him crawled.
His fame reached through the ages.
He skirted the borders of the Kytay;
The enemies who coveted what was his,
Your forefather crushed and burned.
Of the giants who boasted of prowess,
Ogoy devoured them all.
Every living Kyrgyz—
On this account, the people
Called them sons of Ogoy.
While your forefather Ogoy lived,
He summered his people in Ala-Too.
For the mighty who claimed heroic rank,
For those skilled among spearmen,
Before their doorways,
He had a hundred steeds tied apiece.
When enemies came to face him,
He brought their misery to the boil.
He did not sit staring straight ahead.
While hero Ogoy lived,
Those who begged and ate without satisfaction,
Who never gave up their greed—
From among these Kyrgyz people,
He guarded them as a father.
From Khan Ogoy came Khan Bala;
From Khan Bala came Karakan,
When your forefather Karakan died,
That whole people scattered without remainder.
Karakan's eight sons,
The Kara-Kytay and Manzhuu people
Divided and plundered, leaving none.
Wealthy Jakyp went to Altay;
By the Maker's decree, you were born.
Your swift steed to catch and ride—
My child, look at what God has done!
If I pass on the old traditions,
If I ask the knowledgeable,
Those born of the same nest as your father,
Your eight kinsmen, are missing.
From ill-intentioned Jakyp,
You remained, Manas the lion.
When you strike, eighty-four accompany you;
Wherever you strike, red fire blazes.
When your mother bore you in Altay,
Your umbilical blood was shed.
Now to my own eyes,
Your lion's nature has appeared.
Those mortals who obey your word,
You drive forward with commands.
If the enemy will not obey,
You strike straight through and kill them.
At the spurs of ninety mountains,
You are a ridge of strength, my foal.
Of Ogoy the blue-maned, whose name carries weight,
‘A descendant will remain after him,’
We used to discern and know.
It is you, my foal!
You have many mountains where people summer;
Who would split lungs and take the gall,
You have many foes lying in wait.
You have many backs to lean upon;
You have many warriors to bring under your sway.
If you wage battle through the world,
Against a most tormenting enemy,
If you go to face them,
If you measure out the ground,
If you go forth to duel with spears,
When you roar and thrust your spear,
When you stand face to face,
O my dear, the gray horse beneath you—
